newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks to reassure poor countries on trade, aid.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks to reassure poor countries on trade, aid.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday that a planned revision of an important trade and aid pact with a group of mainly former colonies was not a bid to downgrade relations.
The 21-year-old Lome convention, linking the 15-nation EU bloc with 70 countries from black Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific (ACP), is increasingly seen as a colonial hangover.

Initially heralded as a model for cooperation between rich and poor countries, it has become difficult to defend against competing claims from needy Asian and Latin American countries and reforming eastern Europe.

"The main message...is that the EU wants to confirm beyond any doubt that our relationship with ACP countries is something we want to preserve, cherish and deepen," EU development commissioner Joao de Deus Pinheiro told a news conference.
Presenting a discussion paper ahead of the expiry of the Lome pact in February 2000, the EU's Portuguese development aid chief stressed that the partnership would continue.

"In no way should the revision of the Lome convention be seen or considered as something to downgrade our relationship," he said. "On the contrary its main purpose is to find out answers for the 21st century and the challenges we face."
Deus Pinheiro said the aim of the paper was to nourish a wide-ranging debate on how to revitalise relations.

"We have put the problem into an equation but we don't want to solve the problem now," he said, adding that the EU's executive wanted everybody, especially ACP states and private aid agencies, to contribute to the discussion.

Although Africa is often associated with disasters, Deus Pinheiro said there were also success stories, notably in Uganda which was achieving 10 percent economic growth annually and in the Ivory Coast which would soon reach that rate.
But critics point out that despite two decades of trade and aid benefits, ACP states account for 41 out of the world's 50 poorest countries.
Their share of the EU market fell to 2.8 percent in 1994, from 6.7 percent in 1976.
The Commission suggests that greater effort should be made to encourage the private sector and make ACP countries more competitive in world markets.

EU aid must also be made more effective to ensure the continued support of increasingly sceptical European taxpayers who want more resources focused on fighting unemployment and other problems back home.
The global pact could also be split into regional agreements to meet specific economic and political needs of southern Africa, the Caribbean and other areas.
